beats.text: Every morning, someone copies new form entries into a spreadsheet, then pastes a summary into Slack.
Miss one, and a customer never hears back.
What if that busywork ran by itself?
Fix found: Active pieces.
Building blocks for your busywork: when this happens, do that.
Its README calls it an open-source Zapier replacement, with over twenty-five thousand GitHub stars.
Each flow starts with a trigger: a schedule, a webhook, or an event in an app.
Then come the steps, each one a piece: Google Sheets, an A.I. prompt, or a little code.
Test each step, publish, and it runs by itself.
One. Connect your apps: hundreds of ready-made pieces, with loops, branches, retries, and an H.T.T.P. step for the rest.
Two. Keep a human in the loop. A flow can wait, or pause until someone approves, then carry on.
Three. Let your A.I. assistant build it. The built-in M.C.P. server lets Claude or Cursor create flows from a plain request.
Now, the catch.
The core is M.I.T. licensed, but the enterprise code is under a commercial licence. Single sign-on, roles, audit logs and git sync need a paid plan.
The one-command Docker install is for personal use on one machine. Real workloads need a database, a queue, file storage, and a worker for each running flow.
And it's still before version one, so upgrades often bring breaking changes.
It's for teams who want automations on their own servers, and developers happy to write pieces in TypeScript.
If you'd rather not look after a server, it's more than you need.
Want an alternative? Take a look at n-eight-n.
To try it, run the one Docker command from their docs, open it in your browser, and create the first account.
What problem should we fix next? Tell us in the comments.
